extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, news practitioners, and media scholars (and interested newsroom managers/editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive criteria for producing and assessing news content and newsroom practices in a hybrid media system where search engines (especially Google) strongly shape visibility, audience reach, and economic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (technical‑professional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional news values such as recency, conflict, relevance, proximity, and social impact (described as criteria for newsworthiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical‑professional news values are being renegotiated under algorithmic mediation; journalists must consider how such values interact or conflict with algorithmic criteria when selecting and framing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative professional values
rubrics_metrics.description: Core journalistic/professional values (e.g., accuracy, independence, civic mission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists aim to protect these values even while adapting to platform pressures; editorial decisions should be evaluated against these normative commitments rather than purely platform metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic values (engagement and personalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform/algorithmic optimization goals such as engagement, personalization, and metrics that reflect audience behavior (described as algorithmic values and 'mechanical editor' criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These values often privilege click/engagement maximization and can differ from journalistic norms; producers should be aware of how algorithmic optimization incentivizes certain content forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected reception (audience reactions and algorithmic prioritization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A digitally driven news value encompassing anticipated audience experience, engagement behaviors, and algorithmic performance ('expected reception').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection and presentation increasingly factor in expected reception; newsrooms should balance anticipated reception with journalistic purpose and avoid letting it wholly determine coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience metrics as editorial input
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalization of audience preference metrics into newsroom decision making (audience analytics used to guide placement and coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics can substitute for editorial instinct but typically remain under editorial oversight; they can be leveraged strategically but should not uncritically dictate news judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search engine optimization (SEO) / 'search work'
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating content tailored to search engines (segregated content often called 'search work'), including service pieces (e.g., 'the 10 best fish fries') designed to attract search traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEO can increase visibility and is sometimes compatible with civic missions, but there are trade‑offs: some stories are deliberately search‑oriented while others remain high‑quality reporting with different aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide between editorial and commercial
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional newsroom separation between editorial integrity and commercial interests; attention to reach/metrics vs. protecting reporting independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists differ in comfort with engaging metrics; understanding the organization's business model is healthy, but editorial autonomy should be maintained to protect integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / opacity of platform algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived opacity of Google and other platform algorithms ('black box', 'mystery', 'opaque'), limiting journalists' knowledge of how curation and ranking work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opacity complicates prediction and strategy; calls for greater transparency and recognition that algorithm changes require continual monitoring and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of platforms / Google dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: The asymmetric market power of platforms (e.g., Google as an outsized influencer and gatekeeper; 'front page of Google is the front page of our newspaper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize structural effects such as concentration of attention and resources ('rich get richer'); evaluate newsroom strategy and policy responses in light of platform power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmentation of newsroom labor (engagement/digital specialists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational response where engagement editors, SEO specialists, or dedicated teams perform search‑focused or audience work distinct from core reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segmentation formalizes negotiation with platform values; it can protect reporters from optimization pressure but may also embed algorithmic priorities into workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance, Relinquishment, Renegotiation (strategic categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three overlapping strategies journalists deploy toward platforms: resisting algorithmic influence, relinquishing some editorial control (creating search‑oriented content or delegating to specialists), and renegotiating values by reframing reach as civic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to evaluate newsroom responses and their consequences for editorial values, labor division, and public service aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframing visibility as public good / renegotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategy to integrate algorithmic reach into journalistic values by conceiving visibility and distribution as part of civic mission rather than purely commercial goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renegotiation supports selective integration of algorithmic values—newsrooms can treat reach as a means to public service while guarding core editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding clickbait and limits to optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' explicit limits on how far they'll optimize for search/engagement to avoid sensationalist or low‑quality content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should penalize overt clickbaiting; optimization that preserves accuracy and context is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of audience analytics for equitable purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveraging audience data to identify and serve traditionally marginalized audiences (if used with equity goals in mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytics can advance journalistic missions when intentionally directed at inclusion and public interest rather than only monetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donsbach's role dimensions (participant/observational; advocacy/neutral; commercial/educational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework describing journalistic role conceptions: whether journalists influence political processes, express values, or prioritize reach/education ('commercial/educational' increasingly relevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsroom orientation along these axes to understand tensions between public service and audience‑driven imperatives under platform influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms as an external 'mechanical editor' / algorithmic curation
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that search engines operate as external algorithmic editors that curate and prioritize news differently than human editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the normative differences between algorithmic curation and editorial judgment when evaluating content placement and visibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to algorithmic change / continual relearning
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical constraint that platform parameters and ranking behaviors shift, requiring journalists and engagement teams to relearn what 'works'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of newsroom practices should include capacity for iteration, monitoring, and flexibility in response to shifting algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade‑off between traffic‑focused content and high‑quality reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that some content is produced primarily for search/traffic while other pieces prioritize investigative or public‑interest reporting and may attract less reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should explicitly allocate resources and set expectations for different content types rather than letting metrics flatten all editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhancing digital product with multimedia and documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating images, video, embedded documents, and richer digital elements to both improve quality and appeal to digital/algorithmic audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimedia can serve editorial and discoverability goals simultaneously; encourage integration where it genuinely enhances reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic implications of search traffic
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of search‑driven traffic in supporting revenue models (advertising, subscriptions, donations); value of traffic differs by organizational model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate content strategy relative to the organization's revenue priorities (e.g., subscription growth vs. ad volume) and be transparent about how traffic metrics are used by funders and managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and visibility of local and smaller outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that platform curation favors major national sources, exacerbating concentration and marginalizing local reliable outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether platform strategies and advocacy aim to preserve local news visibility and explore practices/policies that elevate trustworthy local sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content performance unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' experience that story success can seem random or surprising due to opaque, shifting algorithmic factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of analytics, experimentation, and editorial judgment rather than assuming deterministic optimization will guarantee consistent success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content management systems (CMS) nudges and embedded routines
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS features and workflow tools that nudge journalists toward search‑friendly content—embedding algorithmic values into everyday production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the impact of production tools on editorial autonomy and consider whether CMS nudges align with the newsroom's editorial standards and public‑service goals.
